what: the drowning net of a sea goddess from an old northern myth, drawn as a heavy coarse net like the cargo net slung from a ship's crane: a lattice of very thick grey silk ropes, each rope as thick as a man's wrist, crossing to make a few huge diamond openings, each opening as big as a man's head; the whole net is only four openings wide and four openings tall, sixteen openings in all, and through every opening the flat backdrop shows clearly. Every crossing of two ropes is bound in a big fat round knot. The net is one single layer with nothing folded behind it, hanging loosely down from one big fat knot at its top centre where its top edge is gathered, its sides and bottom loose and sagging in soft curves. Along the bottom edge hang three round stone sinker weights, each a smooth dull charcoal-grey pebble with a hole bored through it, tied on with the rope, darker than the net. The silk ropes are cold silver-grey with a soft sheen, bright pale silver along the top of every rope and darker slate-grey on the underside.
colours: Cold silver-grey silk ropes, bright pale silver highlights on top of every rope, darker slate-grey underneath, only the faintest cold sea-green sheen on the big top knot; three dull charcoal-grey stone sinkers, darker than the net.
pose: Seen from directly in front, hanging down from its big top knot as if hung in the air, one single layer of coarse net spread open, every opening wide and empty, the whole net inside the picture.
must_show: one coarse net of very thick grey rope with a few huge open holes, the backdrop showing through
big knots where the cords cross, one big knot at the top
small dark grey stone sinkers along the bottom edge
cold silver-grey silk, never brown rope
